tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).

content.content:
1	---
2	name: fortress-repo
3	description: "Use this skill whenever you touch the code of the Fortress language revival (/home/user/fortress or a worktree like fortress-w4): building with ant; recompiling after editing a .fss, .fsi, Java or Scala file; running programs under walk or the bytecode compiler; running or writing tests (testFast, testSystem, harness-one.sh, junit.sh, .test files, XXX expected failures); the gate before landing; editing the interpreter, compiled checker, code generator, Library or Specification; searching the gap ledger or git history; seeding worktrees; committing a code change. Load it before even a small build, test, edit or measurement there, including long background runs you wait on, and when briefing agents for that work; then, for a task that reads or changes the original tree (its Java and Scala, the library, the tests or the specification), or reviews such a change, read references/revival-changes.md whole. Skip it for session upkeep (compaction, boot notes, reading batch results, scheduling agents: coordinator skill, read after this file), Stop hooks, disk or container trouble (cloud-container), other repos, and general Fortress history."
4	---
5	
6	# Working in the Fortress revival repository
7	
8	The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.
9	
10	**curator**
11	: Person in charge of this restoration.
12	
13	**brief**
14	: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.
15	
16	**original tree**
17	: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.
18	
19	**record**
20	: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).
21	
22	**walk**
23	: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.
24	
25	**compiled path**
26	: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.
27	
28	**model program**
29	: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.
30	
31	**one library**
32	: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).
33	
34	**component**
35	: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.
36	
37	**api**
38	: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.
39	
40	**area**
41	: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.
42	
43	**base**
44	: Commit that your work starts from.
45	
46	**gate**
47	: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.
48	
49	**harness**
50	: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.
51	
52	**building**
53	: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.
54	
55	**exploring**
56	: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.
57	
58	You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.
59	
60	## How a program runs
61	
62	Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.
63	
64	### The phases
65	
66	Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):
67	
68	1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
69	2. Bind each name to its declaration.
70	3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
71	4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
72	5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
73	6. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
74	7. Mark each call of an overloaded name.
75	
76	Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.
77	
78	`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.
79	
80	Each path has its own library today. With the environment variable `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `fortress compile` reads the one library instead, and a program compiled so does not run yet (`references/build-and-caches.md`, "The caches"). At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.
81	
82	### The compiled runtime
83	
84	`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:
85	
86	- the component's functions, objects and traits;
87	- its closures;
88	- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.
89	
90	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
91	
92	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
93	
94	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: under the compiler's prelude, an `RR64`'s class extends `FRR64`, which holds the `double`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.
95	
96	### The caches
97	
98	A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, in `default_repository/caches-one/` with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.
99	
100	- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
101	- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
102	- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
103	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.
104	
105	In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).
106	
107	`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.
108	
109	### Parallelism and mutable state
110	
111	Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. 142	
143	The record's main files:
144	
145	- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
146	- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
147	- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
148	- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.
149	
150	Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.
151	
152	## When to explore
153	
154	Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:
155	
156	- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
157	- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
158	- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.
159

162	## Rules for every task

164	- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
6. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
7. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. - its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. - `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).

The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").

- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

## The caches

All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:

- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).

Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).

With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, a run that names no private caches folder uses `default_repository/caches-one` in place of `default_repository/caches`, because a caches folder holds the jars of a single library. Set the environment variable, not only the property `-Dfortress.library=one`. The class path scripts, `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`, read only the variable. With the property alone, the compile writes to `caches-one`, but the run looks in `caches` and prints 'Could not load P'. Run the library order without the variable: it fills `caches` with the prelude's jars. No compile writes the one library's jars yet, so a program compiled with the variable dies at its first library class: 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$String' (ledger row 1062).

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

======

- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised, or a static error of a phase before the run, such as the disambiguator's, counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk misses: it is green while the program loads and runs clean, and red once walk refuses it.

Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:

- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
- `one_library_tests/`: a test whose program compiles against the one library, for a defect that only that library shows. Its tests compile with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, and `ant testOneLibrary` and `testFast` run them. Give a plain test there a `compile` command only: a program compiled so does not run yet (ledger row 1062).
- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series. Put no new test there.

The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:

    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)

A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:

    tests=EqualityRung1
    link
    run
    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

## How `XXX` works

- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. Run the test's program through the harness before you run it any other way. In that Bash call, echo a line that starts `Expected failure:` before the harness command. In that line, say how the harness should report the failure. Then see the test fail that way through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says. If the test passes, or fails another way, find out why and correct it before you make the fix. Then echo the expected failure again in the Bash call that runs the test again. If the run meets a second defect, record it as "How a defect is recorded" says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

In your report, quote each `Expected failure:` line as the call echoed it, two to five lines of each failing run, and the passing line, each run with its command. Give the cause of each run that failed another way. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. content.content:
- a call of a functional method with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all;
- `(r asif T).m(a)`, where `T` overloads `m` and an argument is not an assumption;
- `r.m(a asif U)`, where `r` is not an assumption and `r`'s trait overloads `m`;
- a call of an overloaded function with an assumption at some arguments but not all, where the call can run a functional method of the same name, but not every declaration more specific than the chosen one. An example is `pick(n, b asif Named)` beside an object's `pick(self, y: Named)`.

It also refuses these forms:

- a call of an overloaded function with an assumption at some arguments but not all, where a declaration more specific than the chosen one is generic: 'Can't compile a type assumption at some arguments but not all of a call that a generic declaration can take yet';
- a call of an overloaded function of another component with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded function of another component yet';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded function whose chosen declaration is generic, with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet';
- a call, at an assumption of a generic trait, of a method whose parameter has the trait's type parameter, as `stamp(Q asif Tagged[\String\], s asif String)` for `stamp(self, x: T)` in `Tagged[\T\]`: 'Can't find the body that Tagged[\String\] gives stamp at ...' (ledger row 1088).

At an assumption of a trait, the call runs the trait's body, also where the object overrides it.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. **code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,560 tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
====
To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library: run them with `ant testOneLibrary`.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

====
- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load (`interpreter.md`, "What walk checks").
- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for the bindings in `Library/Reflect.fss`. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
- Check microGPT under walk as `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says.

`ant testFast` runs about 2,560 tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"

I brought eight files of the `fortress-repo` skill in line with climb batch 34b's landing, in one commit. Nothing was installed from the orientation, and I did not push. The lint found nothing in the changed files.

## Commits

- `2d194074ed` "fortress-repo: the parts in line with climb batch 34b's landing". It changes eight files: 44 lines added, 10 removed.

There is no commit for `revival-changes.md`. The orientation update admitted no entry, its judge did not run, and so there was nothing to install.

## Sentences changed, with their reasons

1. **`SKILL.md`, "How a program runs".**
   - Before: the text said that a program compiled with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` "does not run yet". That is now false.
   - Now: "a program compiled so runs against the one library's jars (`references/build-and-caches.md`, "The caches"), but fails at some constructs that walk runs (`references/compiler.md`)."
   - Grounds: F-396; ledger row 1062, now fixed.
2. **`SKILL.md`, "The compiled runtime".**
   - Before: the text limited the rule to the compiler's prelude.
   - Now: "under either library, an `RR64`'s class extends `FRR64`".
   - Grounds: F-388; `NamingCzar.java:637-655`.
3. **`build-and-caches.md`, "The caches".**
   - Before: the text said that no compile writes the one library's jars, so such a program dies at its first library class.
   - Now: "A program compiled with the variable runs only if its caches folder holds the jars of the one library's fourteen components, which `one_library_tests/OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles (`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests")."
   - Grounds: F-396.
4. **`tests-writing.md`, "Where a test goes".**
   - Before: the text said to give a test there a `compile` command only.
   - Now: "A plain run test there runs against the one library's jars, as `OneLibraryRunHello.test` does."
   - Grounds: F-396; I read the `.test` file to confirm it.
5. **`compiler.md`, "What the two paths share".**
   - Before: the text said that only the prelude's number objects extend the run-time number classes.
   - Now: "payload classes that the classes of either library's number objects extend, and under the one library also those of `Boolean`, `Char` and `FlatString`."
   - Grounds: F-388; `NamingCzar.java:637-655`.
6. **`compiler.md`, "The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over".** The part did not say that the run time's classes now come in two sets. Added:
   - "The run time's classes that name a library's types, as `FValue` and `FException`, come in two sets under the same names: `ProjectFortress/build` for the prelude, and `ProjectFortress/build-one`, built from `ProjectFortress/src-one`, for the one library."
   - "With the variable, the class path puts the second set first."
   - "Make a change to a class that both sets hold in both."
   - Grounds: F-396 and F-353; I checked that `src-one/.../runtimeValues/` holds both classes.
7. **`compiler.md`, the varargs paragraph.**
   - Before: the clause was true, but its reason was wrong.
   - Now: "though a program that calls a varargs declaration does not run yet (ledger row 1091)."
   - Grounds: F-390; ledger row 1091.
8. **`compiler.md`, the same section, new.** The part had no list of where a program compiled against the one library fails. Added a list:
   - a call of a varargs declaration (ledger row 1091);
   - a reduction over a range (row 1099);
   - `println` of a number or a boolean (row 1098);
   - `=` and `<` of two strings, and `=` of two booleans (row 994);
   - `u.asString` in a generic body, for `u` of a type parameter bounded by `ZZ32` (row 1101);
   - an uncaught exception, which the run reports with a placeholder (row 1102).

   It also adds: "In one JVM, compile `FortressLibrary` before any other program." The reason is row 1100. Each item gives the error message from its ledger row.
9. **`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path", new.**
   - Added: "On the compiled path, against either library, an exception object without value parameters that a helper raises is a second instance of the object. So in `catch e IntegerOverflow => e SEQV IntegerOverflow`, the comparison is `false`. Walk gives `true` (ledger row 1103)."
   - Grounds: row 1103; F-336; `Utility.java:66-69`.
10. **`interpreter.md`, "Natives".**
    - Before: the text said that a helper names the prelude's whole class, as `"fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero"`. A new helper written that way would raise a class that does not exist under the one library.
    - Now: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("DivisionByZero")`, and "The string is the exception's simple name, and `LibraryNames` maps it to the class of the library in use."
    - Grounds: F-24, F-312 and F-336. I checked the code: `simpleIntArith.java:43`, `Utility.java:34-36`, both `LibraryNames.java` files and walk's `StaticNativeApp.raised`. The text that follows on walk's behaviour stays true.
11. **`tests-running.md`, "The two suites".**
    - Before: "about 2,560 tests ... in about 5 to 7 minutes".
    - Now: "about 2,650 tests ... in about 11 minutes".
    - Grounds: the gate's `summary.txt`. I counted its `testFast` rows by hand: 2,645 tests, 11 minutes 5 seconds.
12. **`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests".**
    - Before: the text said only to run the tests of `one_library_tests/` with `ant testOneLibrary`. It did not say that a run test there needs the fourteen jars.
    - Now: the text says that a run test needs those jars, and gives a list of three ways to run the tests:
      - `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. `ant testSystem` deletes that folder.
      - With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first.
      - For a run by hand, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=$PWD/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`.
    - Grounds: `build.xml:1175-1185`; the rung's report, "Commands worked out"; `junit.sh:27-31`.
13. **`library.md`, "Designing a change".**
    - Before: an edit of the fourteen components had no compiled step.
    - Now: "For any of the fourteen, also `ant testOneLibrary`. Its `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles them, so it also fails on a declaration that the code generator refuses."
    - Grounds: F-34.

`sources.md` has a new section, "Climb batch 34b's landing, 2026-11-21", with one line for each change.

- **The `coordinator` skill's "Quiet times" (P-164).** If it needs a change, that change is yours.
- **A fault of the data: the "fourteen" components.** The review says that `OneShotFlag` is "outside the distance stage's fourteen apis". F-53 and `OneLibraryComponents.test` both include `OneShotFlag`. The skill follows F-53.
